clinicalPearls: A benign fibro-osseous lesion with a strong predilection for the anterior cortex of the tibial diaphysis in infants and children
Often presents as painless anterior bowing of the tibia or an incidental radiographic finding
Radiographs show an intracortical, well-defined lytic lesion with surrounding sclerosis and characteristic anterior tibial bowing
Histology shows a fibrous stroma with woven bone trabeculae rimmed by osteoblasts, distinguishing it from fibrous dysplasia where osteoblastic rimming is absent
Shares a close relationship with adamantinoma, and OFD-like adamantinoma sits on a spectrum, so careful assessment for epithelial cells is essential
Immunohistochemistry may reveal scattered keratin-positive cells, raising concern for an adamantinomatous component
Given the tendency to recur in young children, observation is often preferred until skeletal maturity unless there is deformity or fracture
reference.pathophysiology: Osteofibrous dysplasia is a benign fibro-osseous proliferation confined largely to the cortex of the tibia, and less often the fibula. The lesion is composed of a bland fibroblastic stroma containing irregular trabeculae of woven bone that, in contrast to fibrous dysplasia, are lined by prominent osteoblasts. It is developmentally and biologically linked to adamantinoma, and lesions exist along a continuum from pure osteofibrous dysplasia through OFD-like adamantinoma to classic adamantinoma, defined by the extent of an epithelial component. Cortical weakening produces the characteristic anterior bowing of the tibia.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiography to demonstrate the intracortical lytic lesion and tibial bowing
MRI to assess extent and to look for features concerning for adamantinoma
Histology with attention to osteoblastic rimming of bony trabeculae
Cytokeratin immunohistochemistry to detect scattered or clustered epithelial cells
Long-term radiographic surveillance to monitor for progression or adamantinomatous change
redFlags: Increasing size or pain suggesting progression to adamantinoma
Identification of a substantial epithelial component on biopsy
Progressive deformity or pathological fracture of the tibia
Recurrence after resection in an older child or adult
reference.prognosis: Osteofibrous dysplasia is benign and frequently stabilises or regresses around skeletal maturity, but it recurs readily after excision in young children. Its principal significance lies in its relationship to adamantinoma, which mandates careful histological assessment and follow-up.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude an adamantinomatous component through inadequate sampling or absent keratin staining
Confusing it with fibrous dysplasia by overlooking the osteoblastic rimming
Performing aggressive early resection that is prone to recurrence in young children
Attributing anterior tibial bowing solely to developmental causes without imaging
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Osteofibrous dysplasia is usually a benign, self-limited lesion in children, so the default posture is watchful observation rather than early intervention
Asymptomatic or incidentally found lesions in a growing child are followed with serial radiographs, since many stabilise or regress as the child nears skeletal maturity
Anterior tibial bowing without progressive deformity, fracture, or significant pain is managed with continued observation, protective bracing, and activity modification rather than surgery

Progressive deformity, recurrent or impending pathological fracture, or a lesion that fails to stabilise near skeletal maturity warrants corrective surgery, typically curettage or resection with bone grafting or osteotomy for established deformity

Any biopsy finding suggestive of an epithelial keratin-positive component (OFD-like or classic adamantinoma) shifts management toward that of a low- to intermediate-grade bone malignancy, with wide surgical resection rather than observation

Surgery in pure osteofibrous dysplasia is reserved rather than first-line, since resection in young children carries a high recurrence rate, and is generally deferred until closer to skeletal maturity when undertaken

Adequate tissue sampling at biopsy or resection is essential so an epithelial component is not missed, since this determines whether the lesion is treated as benign disease or as adamantinoma-spectrum disease
There is no established role for radiotherapy or systemic cytotoxic, targeted, or immune therapy in osteofibrous dysplasia itself
If histology confirms transformation along the adamantinoma spectrum, treatment intent and modality follow that of the malignant entity, managed as a bone sarcoma with surgery as the mainstay
Serial clinical and radiographic follow-up through childhood and adolescence tracks lesion behaviour, tibial bowing, and any radiographic change
Long-term surveillance is warranted given the relationship to adamantinoma, and any increase in size, new pain, or concerning radiographic change should prompt re-biopsy
After any surgical intervention, continued follow-up for recurrence is needed, since recurrence is more common when resection is performed at a young age

Refer to an orthopaedic oncology service for biopsy planning where adamantinoma cannot be excluded, progressive tibial deformity or fracture risk requiring surgical correction, or any keratin-positive epithelial finding on histology
Musculoskeletal pathology review with cytokeratin immunohistochemistry is warranted whenever the epithelial question is unresolved on initial biopsy
